notes: Reasoning Ability topic package 2 for BATCH_009 (Month and Date-Based Puzzles, Puzzles (Other), Syllogism, Inequality): 57 original questions built by tools/packages/REAS_pkg2.py. Puzzles are brute-forced for a unique arrangement or recomputed with datetime; syllogisms checked over every Venn-region model; inequalities over every integer ordering (with a wider-range cross-check).

stimuli.title: Five Greek capital letters for comparisons
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, the Greek capital letters Γ, Λ, Ξ, Π and Ψ are used with these meanings:
'A Γ B' means 'A is greater than B'; 'A Λ B' means 'A is smaller than B'; 'A Ξ B' means 'A is either greater than or equal to B'; 'A Π B' means 'A is either smaller than or equal to B'; 'A Ψ B' means 'A is equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Decode: Γ means >, Λ means <, Ξ means ≥, Π means ≤ and Ψ means =. Rewrite the statements with ordinary signs, join them into a chain and test each conclusion.

stimuli.title: Five chess symbols defined by negations
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, chess symbols are used between two letters with these meanings:
'A ♔ B' means 'A is neither smaller than nor equal to B'; 'A ♕ B' means 'A is not greater than B'; 'A ♖ B' means 'A is neither greater than nor smaller than B'; 'A ♗ B' means 'A is not smaller than B'; 'A ♘ B' means 'A is neither greater than nor equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Translate each negation: 'neither smaller nor equal' = >, 'not greater' = ≤, 'neither greater nor smaller' = =, 'not smaller' = ≥, 'neither greater nor equal' = <. So ♔ is >, ♕ is ≤, ♖ is =, ♗ is ≥ and ♘ is <. Then join the statements into one chain.

stimuli.title: Six treks in six months, read by season
stimuli.content:
Six friends Aadi, Bela, Daksh, Hema, Ishan and Kajal each go on one trek in the same year, in six different months among January, March, April, July, October and December. Take the seasons as: Spring = January to March, Summer = April to June, Monsoon = July to September, Winter = October to December.

- Hema treks in the only Summer month among the six.
- Ishan treks in a Monsoon month.
- Kajal treks in the month that comes just before Hema's among the six months.
- Daksh and Bela both trek in Winter, and Bela's month is later.
stimuli.solution:
Of the six months, only April is in Summer: Hema. Only July is in Monsoon: Ishan. The month before April in the list is March: Kajal. Winter months are October and December; Bela is later, so Daksh October and Bela December. Aadi takes the remaining month, January.

Jan Aadi, Mar Kajal, Apr Hema, Jul Ishan, Oct Daksh, Dec Bela.

stimuli.title: Six appointments across the end of September 2026
stimuli.content:
Six persons Pranav, Rukmini, Sachin, Tanvi, Uttam and Vidya each have one appointment at a passport office on six different dates from Friday, 25 September 2026 to Tuesday, 6 October 2026 (September has 30 days).

- Rukmini's appointment is on the last day of September.
- Pranav's appointment is exactly five days after Rukmini's.
- Tanvi's appointment is on the first Saturday of the period.
- Vidya's appointment is on a Friday in October.
- Sachin's appointment is on the day after Vidya's.
- Uttam's appointment is on a Monday, before Rukmini's.
stimuli.solution:
Days: Fri 25, Sat 26, Sun 27, Mon 28, Tue 29, Wed 30 September; Thu 1, Fri 2, Sat 3, Sun 4, Mon 5, Tue 6 October. Rukmini 30 September; Pranav five days later, 5 October. Tanvi: first Saturday, 26 September. Vidya: the Friday in October, 2 October; Sachin 3 October. Uttam: a Monday before 30 September, 28 September.

Tanvi 26 Sep (Sat), Uttam 28 Sep (Mon), Rukmini 30 Sep (Wed), Vidya 2 Oct (Fri), Sachin 3 Oct (Sat), Pranav 5 Oct (Mon).

stimuli.title: Six employees and their retirement years
stimuli.content:
Six employees Gyan, Hridya, Kesar, Lohit, Mrinal and Navya of a bank were born in six different years between 1960 and 1995. Each employee retires in the year in which he or she turns 60.

- Kesar retires in 2031.
- Lohit is seven years younger than Kesar.
- Gyan retires in 2026, and Navya is exactly ten years younger than Gyan.
- Hridya was born in a leap year, after Kesar but before Lohit.
- Mrinal is the youngest of the six, and Mrinal's age in 2026 is a perfect square.
stimuli.solution:
Kesar: 2031 − 60 = 1971; Lohit 1978. Gyan: 2026 − 60 = 1966; Navya 1976. Hridya: a leap year after 1971 and before 1978 — 1972 or 1976 — and 1976 is Navya's, so 1972. Mrinal is the youngest (after 1978) and is a perfect-square age in 2026: 36 (born 1990) is the only one within 1979–1995 (25 would be 2001, 49 would be 1977).

Birth / retirement: Gyan 1966/2026, Kesar 1971/2031, Hridya 1972/2032, Navya 1976/2036, Lohit 1978/2038, Mrinal 1990/2050.

stimuli.title: Three departments, two posts each, six joining years
stimuli.content:
Six employees Aarav, Bhakti, Chaitali, Devesh, Eeshan and Fiza work in three departments of a company — HR, IT and Sales. Each holds one of two posts, Manager or Executive, and each joined in a different year from 2018 to 2023.

- Each department has exactly two of them: one Manager and one Executive, and in each department the Manager joined earlier than the Executive.
- Aarav, an Executive, joined last of the six.
- Devesh joined first of the six, and Bhakti works in the same department as Devesh.
- Fiza is a Manager and joined one year after Devesh.
- Chaitali works in Sales and joined in 2020.
- Eeshan joined in the year after Chaitali and works in the same department as her.
- Bhakti does not work in IT.
stimuli.solution:
Aarav joined in 2023 as an Executive; Devesh in 2018. Devesh joined before everyone, so he cannot be an Executive (his Manager would have joined earlier): Devesh is a Manager, and Bhakti, in his department, is its Executive. Fiza: Manager, 2019. Chaitali: Sales, 2020; Eeshan: Sales, 2021 — so Chaitali is the Sales Manager and Eeshan the Sales Executive. Sales is full, so Devesh and Bhakti are in HR or IT; Bhakti is not in IT, so both are in HR. Fiza then manages IT and Aarav is the IT Executive. Bhakti takes the remaining year, 2022.

HR: Devesh (Manager, 2018), Bhakti (Executive, 2022); IT: Fiza (Manager, 2019), Aarav (Executive, 2023); Sales: Chaitali (Manager, 2020), Eeshan (Executive, 2021).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
All monkeys are bears.
Some rabbits are not bears.

Conclusions:
I. Some bears are rabbits.
II. Some rabbits are not monkeys.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: Some rabbits lie outside the bears; every monkey is inside the bears, so those rabbits are not monkeys (II). Whether any bear is a rabbit is open (I).
steps: Rabbits outside bears are outside monkeys (monkeys ⊂ bears) ⇒ II follows
Bears and rabbits need not overlap ⇒ I not certain
solution.why_others_wrong: Conclusion I is not forced by the statements (some valid diagram breaks it), so 'Both' and 'Only I' are wrong; II holds in every diagram, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
No squirrel is a dolphin.
All whales are dolphins.

Conclusions:
I. No whale is a squirrel.
II. Some dolphins are not squirrels.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: Whales ⊂ dolphins and dolphins never meet squirrels, so no whale is a squirrel (I). Since no dolphin is a squirrel and dolphins exist, some dolphins are not squirrels (II).
steps: All whales are dolphins + No dolphin is a squirrel ⇒ No whale is a squirrel: I
No dolphin is a squirrel ⇒ some dolphins are not squirrels: II
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion holds in every valid diagram, so choosing only one of them, or neither, is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
Some yaks are not goats.
All donkeys are goats.

Conclusions:
I. Some yaks are donkeys.
II. No yak is a donkey.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Either conclusion I or II follows

solution.explanation: The statements leave the yak–donkey relation open: yaks may or may not reach into the goats (where the donkeys are). So neither I nor II is certain, but they are a complementary pair: one must be true.
steps: No definite yak–donkey relation
'Some yaks are donkeys' / 'No yak is a donkey' ⇒ complementary pair
Either I or II follows
solution.why_others_wrong: Neither conclusion is certain alone, so 'Only I' and 'Only II' are wrong; but in every diagram one of the two holds, so 'Neither' is wrong. ('Either' replaces 'Both' under the four-option rule.)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
Only muffins are biscuits.
No samosa is a muffin.

Conclusions:
I. No biscuit is a samosa.
II. All muffins are biscuits.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: 'Only muffins are biscuits' means every biscuit is a muffin. Muffins never meet samosas, so no biscuit is a samosa (I). The statement does not say every muffin is a biscuit (II) — that would be 'Only biscuits are muffins'.
steps: Only muffins are biscuits ⇒ biscuits ⊂ muffins
Muffins ∩ samosas = ∅ ⇒ I follows
Muffins may extend beyond biscuits ⇒ II not certain
solution.why_others_wrong: Conclusion II is not forced by the statements (some valid diagram breaks it), so 'Both' and 'Only II' are wrong; I holds in every diagram, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
Only a few laddoos are jalebis.
Only a few dosas are jalebis.

Conclusions:
I. Some laddoos are dosas.
II. All jalebis are laddoos.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: Laddoos and dosas each overlap the jalebis only partly, and their overlaps may be different parts, so 'Some laddoos are dosas' is not certain (I). The jalebis meeting the dosas may lie outside the laddoos, so 'All jalebis are laddoos' is not certain either (II).
steps: Two 'Only a few' statements with the middle term as predicate ⇒ no laddoo–dosa link
Jalebi ∩ dosa may avoid laddoos ⇒ II not certain
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails in at least one valid diagram, so 'Only I', 'Only II' and 'Both' are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
All pizzas are burgers.
Only a few noodles are burgers.

Conclusions:
I. All noodles being pizzas is a possibility.
II. All burgers being noodles is a possibility.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: Some noodles are not burgers, and every pizza is a burger, so those noodles are not pizzas: all noodles can never be pizzas (I fails). The burgers may all lie inside the noodles — only a few noodles being burgers is still satisfied — so II is possible.
steps: Noodles outside burgers are outside pizzas ⇒ I impossible
Burgers ⊂ noodles keeps 'only a few noodles are burgers' true ⇒ II possible
solution.why_others_wrong: Conclusion I is not forced by the statements (some valid diagram breaks it), so 'Both' and 'Only I' are wrong; II holds in every diagram, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
No soup is a salad.
Some salads are sandwiches.

Taking the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, which one of the following conclusions definitely follows?

options.text: All sandwiches being soups is a possibility.
All salads being soups is a possibility.
Some soups being sandwiches is a possibility.

solution.explanation: The sandwiches outside the salads are unrestricted, so some of them may be soups: 'Some soups being sandwiches is a possibility' follows.
steps: Soups only avoid salads
Sandwiches outside salads may meet soups ⇒ possible
solution.why_others_wrong: All sandwiches can never be soups (some sandwiches are salads); all salads being soups contradicts 'No soup is a salad'; 'Some sandwiches are soups' is possible but not definite.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Some soups being sandwiches is a possibility.

questions.question_text:

Some snakes are frogs.
No frog is a turtle.

Conclusions:

II. Some snakes are not turtles.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

steps: Lizards ⊂ snakes may fall inside snake ∩ frog ⇒ I possible
Snake ∩ frog ≠ ∅ and outside turtles ⇒ II definite
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion holds in every valid diagram, so choosing only one of them, or neither, is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: B ≤ R = E < Y ≥ P > L

Conclusions:
I. B < Y
II. L < E

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: B ≤ R = E < Y gives B < Y (I). L < P ≤ Y and then the chain turns at Y (E < Y), so L and E are unrelated (II).
steps: I: B ≤ R = E < Y ⇒ B < Y, true
II: E < Y ≥ P > L: turn at Y ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: II is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only II' and 'Both' are wrong; I always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: S > F ≥ A < C = O ≤ U

Conclusions:
I. S > C
II. U > A

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: S > F ≥ A < C turns at A, so S and C are unrelated (I). U ≥ O = C > A gives U > A (II).
steps: I: turn at A ⇒ no relation
II: U ≥ O = C > A ⇒ U > A, true
solution.why_others_wrong: I is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only I' and 'Both' are wrong; II always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: Y ≥ M = G ≤ X < K > I

Conclusions:
I. Y ≥ X
II. I < X

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: Y ≥ M = G ≤ X turns at G, so Y and X are unrelated (I). X < K > I turns at K, so I and X are unrelated (II).
steps: I: turn at G ⇒ no relation
II: turn at K ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails for some ordering that satisfies the statements, so the other three are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither I nor II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: N < W ≤ J ≤ H = D < Z

Conclusions:
I. N < H
II. Z > J

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: Every sign points the same way. N < W ≤ J ≤ H gives N < H (I); Z > D = H ≥ J gives Z > J (II).
steps: I: N < W ≤ J ≤ H ⇒ N < H, true
II: Z > D = H ≥ J ⇒ Z > J, true
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion holds for every ordering that satisfies the statements, so picking one, or neither, is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: T Π K, K Ψ B, B Γ U

Conclusions:
I. T Λ B
II. T Ψ B

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Either I or II is true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: T ≤ K = B > U, so T ≤ B. T < B and T = B are each uncertain, but one of them must hold.
steps: Decode: T ≤ K, K = B, B > U
T ≤ K = B ⇒ T ≤ B
I (T < B) and II (T = B) split '≤' ⇒ either
solution.why_others_wrong: Neither conclusion is certain alone, but one of them must hold, so 'Neither' is wrong. ('Either' replaces 'Both' under the four-option rule.)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either I or II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

Statements: R Ξ H, H Γ M, M Π D

Conclusions:
I. R Γ M
II. D Γ H

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: R ≥ H > M ≤ D. R > M follows (I). D and H are on opposite sides of the turn at M, so D > H is not certain (II).
steps: Decode: R ≥ H, H > M, M ≤ D
I: R ≥ H > M ⇒ R > M, true
II: turn at M ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: II is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only II' and 'Both' are wrong; I always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only I is true

Statements: Z Λ Q, Q Ψ C, C Ξ F

I. Z Λ F
II. Q Ξ F

options.text: Neither I nor II is true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: Z < Q = C ≥ F. Z and F lie on opposite sides of the turn at Q = C, so Z < F is not certain (I). Q = C ≥ F gives Q ≥ F (II).
steps: Decode: Z < Q, Q = C, C ≥ F
I: turn at C ⇒ no relation
II: Q = C ≥ F ⇒ Q ≥ F, true
solution.why_others_wrong: I is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only I' and 'Both' are wrong; II always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.

steps: Decode: A > W, W = E, E < V
I: A > W = E < V: turn at E ⇒ no relation
II: W < V ⇒ W > V false
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails for some ordering that satisfies the statements, so the other three are wrong.

I: P > A, true
II: C < A ≤ Y < X ⇒ C < X, true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: D ≥ K; K < R; R ≤ W; W = Q; L > D

Conclusions:
I. L > R
II. Q > D

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: Combined: L > D ≥ K < R ≤ W = Q. Both conclusions compare a term left of K with a term right of K, and the chain turns at K (D ≥ K < R).
steps: Chain: L > D ≥ K < R ≤ W = Q
I and II cross the turn at K ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails for some ordering that satisfies the statements, so the other three are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither I nor II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: F = V; V > N; N ≥ B; G ≥ B; G < I

Conclusions:
I. F > G
II. I > B

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: Combined: F = V > N ≥ B ≤ G < I. F and G are on opposite sides of the turn at B, so F > G is not certain (I). I > G ≥ B gives I > B (II).
steps: Chain: F = V > N ≥ B ≤ G < I
I: turn at B ⇒ no relation
II: I > G ≥ B ⇒ I > B, true
solution.why_others_wrong: I is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only I' and 'Both' are wrong; II always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: J ♗ R, R ♖ W, W ♔ E, S ♕ E, S ♘ M

Conclusions:
I. J ♔ W
II. J ♖ W

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Either I or II is true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: J ≥ R = W > E ≥ S < M. Only J ≥ W is known, so J > W and J = W are each uncertain, but one must hold.
steps: Decode: J ≥ R, R = W, W > E, S ≤ E, S < M
J ≥ R = W ⇒ J ≥ W
I (J > W) and II (J = W) split '≥' ⇒ either
solution.why_others_wrong: Neither conclusion is certain alone, but one of them must hold, so 'Neither' is wrong. ('Either' replaces 'Both' under the four-option rule.)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either I or II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: U ♘ N, N ♕ T, T ♖ I, I ♘ O, Y ♗ O

Conclusions:
I. U ♘ I
II. Y ♔ N

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: U < N ≤ T = I < O ≤ Y. U < I (I) and Y ≥ O > I = T ≥ N gives Y > N (II).
steps: Decode: U < N, N ≤ T, T = I, I < O, Y ≥ O
Chain: U < N ≤ T = I < O ≤ Y
I: U < I, true
II: Y > N, true
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion holds for every ordering that satisfies the statements, so picking one, or neither, is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: H ♔ L, L ♗ F, F ♘ D, D ♖ P, K ♗ D

Conclusions:
I. H ♔ D
II. K ♗ L

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: H > L ≥ F < D = P ≤ K. Both conclusions compare a term left of F with a term right of F, and the chain turns at F.
steps: Decode: H > L, L ≥ F, F < D, D = P, K ≥ D
Chain: H > L ≥ F < D = P ≤ K
I and II cross the turn at F ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails for some ordering that satisfies the statements, so the other three are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither I nor II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: C ♕ G, G ♘ A, A ♗ B, B ♔ X, X ♖ Z

Conclusions:
I. A ♔ Z
II. C ♘ B

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: C ≤ G < A ≥ B > X = Z. A ≥ B > X = Z gives A > Z (I). C and B are on opposite sides of the turn at A, so C < B is not certain (II).
steps: Decode: C ≤ G, G < A, A ≥ B, B > X, X = Z
I: A > Z, true
II: turn at A ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: II is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only II' and 'Both' are wrong; I always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: Q ≥ E; E > I; I = H; H ≤ V; V < T; W ≥ Q

Conclusions:
I. W > V
II. T > I

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: Combined: W ≥ Q ≥ E > I = H ≤ V < T. W and V are on opposite sides of the turn at H, so W > V is not certain (I). T > V ≥ H = I gives T > I (II).
steps: Chain: W ≥ Q ≥ E > I = H ≤ V < T
I: turn at H ⇒ no relation
II: T > V ≥ H = I ⇒ T > I, true
solution.why_others_wrong: I is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only I' and 'Both' are wrong; II always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: K < D; D ≤ P; P = Y; Y > G; G ≥ N; N > Z

Conclusions:
I. K < G
II. P > N
III. Z < P

Which of the conclusions is/are definitely true?

options.text: Only II and III are true
All I, II and III are true
None of I, II and III is true

solution.concept: Three conclusions tested against one chain
solution.explanation: Combined: K < D ≤ P = Y > G ≥ N > Z. K and G lie on opposite sides of the turn at Y, so K < G is not certain (I). P = Y > G ≥ N gives P > N (II), and Z < N ≤ G < Y = P gives Z < P (III).
steps: Chain: K < D ≤ P = Y > G ≥ N > Z
I: turn at Y ⇒ not certain
II: P > N, true
III: Z < P, true
Only II and III
solution.why_others_wrong: 'All three' accepts I, which crosses the turn at Y; 'Only II' misses III; 'None' misses both.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only II and III are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In which of the following expressions is 'M ≥ C' definitely true, but 'M > C' not definitely true?

solution.concept: '≥' certain but '>' not: the path must avoid every strict sign
solution.explanation: In M ≥ T = R ≥ C ≤ B, the path from M to C has only '≥' and '=' signs, so M ≥ C is certain but M = C is still possible — M > C is not certain.
steps: Need: path M → C with no turn and no strict sign
M ≥ T = R ≥ C: only ≥ and = ⇒ M ≥ C, not M > C
solution.why_others_wrong: M ≥ T > R = C and B ≤ M > T = R ≥ C contain a strict sign, so M > C is definitely true as well; M = T ≥ R ≤ C turns at R, so even M ≥ C is not certain.
solution.final_answer: Option B: M ≥ T = R ≥ C ≤ B

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In a certain month, the 14th is a Wednesday. Leena's birthday is on the 14th. Manas's birthday is three days after Leena's, and Nirav's birthday is on the Monday of the same week (the week runs from Monday to Sunday).

On which date is Nirav's birthday, and on which day of the week is Manas's birthday?

solution.explanation: The Monday of the week that holds Wednesday the 14th is two days earlier: the 12th. Manas: 14 + 3 = 17th; Wednesday + 3 days = Saturday.
steps: Wednesday 14 ⇒ Monday 12
Manas: 17th = Wednesday + 3 = Saturday
solution.why_others_wrong: 13th is a Tuesday; Friday is the 16th, only two days after Leena's; 11th is the Sunday of the previous week.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

Four siblings Jugal, Kirti, Lakshmi and Mohan were born in 2001, 2004, 2007 and 2010, one in each year. Ages are counted in completed years on their birthdays.

How old will Mohan be on his birthday in 2026?

solution.explanation: Kirti is the eldest: 2001. Jugal is older than Mohan, who is older than Lakshmi: Jugal 2004, Mohan 2007, Lakshmi 2010. In 2026 Mohan turns 2026 − 2007 = 19.
steps: Kirti 2001
Jugal 2004, Mohan 2007, Lakshmi 2010

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

Four friends Rina, Sohan, Tara and Uday each start a monthly savings plan in a different month of the same year.

- Sohan starts four months after Rina.
- Tara starts two months before Sohan.
- Uday starts in the month immediately after Tara's.

Who starts in June?

solution.explanation: Rina: March. Sohan: March + 4 = July. Tara: July − 2 = May. Uday: May + 1 = June.
steps: Rina Mar ⇒ Sohan Jul ⇒ Tara May ⇒ Uday Jun
solution.why_others_wrong: Tara starts in May, Sohan in July and Rina in March.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Seven persons Gagan, Heer, Ikram, Jaya, Kanta, Lucky and Manav each go grocery shopping on one of seven consecutive days, from a Wednesday to the following Tuesday, one person per day.
- Exactly three persons shop between Heer and Kanta, and Heer shops before Kanta.
- Ikram shops on Saturday, and Jaya on the day immediately after Ikram.
- Manav shops on the first of the seven days.
- Gagan shops later than Lucky.
- Kanta does not shop on the last of the seven days.

Who shops on Friday?

solution.explanation: Days 1–7 are Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun, Mon, Tue. Manav Wed, Ikram Sat, Jaya Sun. Heer and Kanta are four days apart: (Thu, Mon) or (Fri, Tue); Kanta is not on Tuesday, so Heer Thu and Kanta Mon. Friday and Tuesday remain; Gagan is later than Lucky, so Lucky shops on Friday and Gagan on Tuesday.
steps: Manav Wed, Ikram Sat, Jaya Sun
Heer–Kanta 4 apart, Kanta ≠ Tue ⇒ Heer Thu, Kanta Mon
Lucky Fri, Gagan Tue
solution.why_others_wrong: Gagan shops on Tuesday, Heer on Thursday and Kanta on Monday.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Lucky

Six cyclists Ritesh, Sonal, Tara, Umang, Vipin and Wahida rode at different speeds in a race.
- Ritesh is faster than exactly two of the others.
- Sonal is faster than Ritesh.
- Tara is slower than Umang but faster than Sonal.
- Vipin is not the slowest.

Who is the second slowest?

solution.concept: Use 'exactly' counts to fix a position
solution.explanation: Umang > Tara > Sonal > Ritesh, and Ritesh is faster than exactly two cyclists — Vipin and Wahida, the only ones left. Vipin is not the slowest, so Wahida is last and Vipin second slowest.
steps: Umang > Tara > Sonal > Ritesh
Two below Ritesh: Vipin, Wahida
Vipin not last ⇒ Vipin 5th (second slowest)
solution.why_others_wrong: Ritesh is the third slowest, Wahida the slowest and Sonal the fourth slowest.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Vipin

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Seven persons Nikhil, Pooja, Rehana, Sameer, Tavleen, Uday and Vaani each visit an art gallery on a different day of one week, from Monday to Sunday.
- As many persons visit before Nikhil as visit after Pooja.
- Exactly two persons visit between Nikhil and Rehana.
- Sameer visits on Thursday, and Rehana visits after Sameer.
- Tavleen visits after Uday, and exactly one person visits between Uday and Sameer.
- Vaani visits before Nikhil.

Who visits on the day immediately before Rehana?

solution.explanation: Let Nikhil be day n and Pooja day p: n − 1 = 7 − p, so n + p = 8. Rehana is after Thursday (5, 6 or 7) and three days from Nikhil, so Nikhil is on day 2, 3 or 4; day 4 is Sameer's. Uday is two days from Sameer: day 2 or 6. Case Nikhil 2: Pooja 6, Rehana 5, Vaani 1, Uday must be 6 — taken by Pooja ✗. Case Nikhil 3: Pooja 5, Rehana 6, Uday 2 (day 6 is Rehana's), Tavleen after Uday and Vaani before Nikhil leave Vaani Monday and Tavleen Sunday. So: Mon Vaani, Tue Uday, Wed Nikhil, Thu Sameer, Fri Pooja, Sat Rehana, Sun Tavleen. The day before Rehana's is Pooja's.
steps: Nikhil + Pooja = 8; Rehana ∈ {5, 6, 7} and |Nikhil − Rehana| = 3
Nikhil 2 ⇒ Uday has no day ✗
Nikhil 3 ⇒ Pooja 5, Rehana 6, Uday 2, Vaani 1, Tavleen 7
Before Saturday (Rehana): Friday ⇒ Pooja
solution.why_others_wrong: Sameer is on Thursday, Tavleen on Sunday (after Rehana) and Nikhil on Wednesday.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Pooja

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five students Ketan, Lavi, Mansi, Neha and Oindrila took two tests. In each test they got the ranks 1 to 5 (rank 1 is the best), with no ties.
- No student has the same rank in both tests.
- The student ranked 1st in Test 1 is ranked 3rd in Test 2.
- Lavi's rank in Test 2 is exactly two places better than in Test 1.
- Oindrila is 2nd in Test 1 and last in Test 2.
- Ketan's two ranks add up to 6.
- Neha is ranked below Ketan in both tests.

Who is ranked 4th in Test 2?

solution.explanation: Oindrila: (2, 5). Ketan's ranks add to 6: (1, 5) and (2, 4) clash with Oindrila, (3, 3) repeats a rank, and (5, 1) leaves no room for Neha below Ketan in Test 1 — so Ketan is (4, 2). Neha is below Ketan in both: Test 1 rank 5, Test 2 rank 3 or 4. Lavi improves by two: Test 1 rank 3 → Test 2 rank 1 (rank 1 in Test 1 cannot improve). Mansi takes Test 1 rank 1 and so Test 2 rank 3, leaving Neha 4th in Test 2.
steps: Oindrila (2, 5)
Ketan (4, 2): the other sums fail
Neha (5, ·); Lavi (3, 1)
Mansi (1, 3) ⇒ Neha (5, 4)
solution.why_others_wrong: Ketan is 2nd in Test 2, Mansi 3rd and Lavi 1st.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Neha
